title: Charles Darwin Loses His Daughter Annie
text:
Anne Elizabeth Darwin, called Annie, was the second child and eldest daughter of Charles and Emma Darwin. She was lively and affectionate, and her father adored her. In 1850, at nine, she began to fall ill with a fever and sickness that would not go away.

In March 1851 Darwin took her to Malvern for the water cure of Dr James Gully, which he had tried himself. She seemed to improve, then grew worse. Darwin hurried back to her side, while Emma, heavily pregnant, stayed at home at Down House. For days he sat with her and wrote anxious letters to Emma describing every change. Annie died on 23 April 1851, at the age of ten. Darwin was too distraught to stay for the funeral.

A week later he wrote a private memorial of her, describing her joy, her tenderness and the way she used to fling herself into his arms. "We have lost the joy of the household, and the solace of our old age," he wrote. "She must have known how we loved her."

Darwin's biographers believe the loss did much to end what remained of his Christian faith, since he could no longer reconcile her death with a loving God. Emma kept a small box of Annie's things. Generations later, his great-great-grandson Randal Keynes used it as the starting point of a book about the family.
lesson: Grief for a child can reshape everything we believe. Writing down what we loved about someone can help us keep them.
people: Charles Darwin, Emma Darwin, Annie Darwin
location: Malvern and Down House, Kent, England (UK)
source: Charles Darwin, memorial of Anne Elizabeth Darwin (30 April 1851), Darwin Correspondence Project; Randal Keynes, Annie's Box (2001)
caveat: How far Annie's death, rather than his scientific work, ended Darwin's faith is a matter of interpretation.
